name: Mythic Tale
summary: A myth, legend or sacred story performed by a visible storyteller: lamp-lit paper diorama, the tradition's own art as duotoned museum plates, gods and heroes identified by their iconography, the text and version named. Reverent, handmade and never preaching or debunking.

visual_job.viewer_leaves_able_to: Retell the episode as this tradition tells it, recognise its god or hero by their emblems, and say which text it comes from.
visual_job.hero: One god, hero or sage, identified by attributes, mount or emblem, framed by a halo, niche or arch inside a layered paper world.

use_when: The film retells a myth, legend, epic episode, Jataka, Tirthankara life or origin story.
The tradition's own art (sculpture, manuscripts, vases, picture stones, folk painting) can carry the look.
The stance is storyteller: 'as told in', neither devotional nor debunking.
avoid_when: The film argues whether events happened (use chronicle or news-brief with evidence).
The subject is a living religious practice or a current controversy (use news-brief).
No one on the team can check the iconography and the telling before release.

alternates.when: Action-led episodes (battles, journeys, chases) or a narrator-puppet frame; traditions with shadow theatre (Tholu Bommalata, Togalu Gombeyata, Karagiozis).
The tradition has a strong painted manuscript, scroll or frieze form to follow (Pattachitra, Kalpasutra, Phad, kaavad, black- and red-figure vases).
The story is best told through surviving artefacts: temple sculpture, Greek vases, Roman reliefs, Gotland picture stones.
Only when the brief explicitly asks for night or dread (Ragnarok, Kali's battle); dark themes are opt-in.

scene_grammar.formula: The storyteller's frame: lamp, ornament border and the source cartouche ('As told in the Valmiki Ramayana'), with the first image of the story on screen inside the hook window.
The cosmos, kingdom or forest as a paper diorama: three or more planes placed by hand, a slow push with parallax.

The god or hero appears, identified by iconography (attributes, mount, emblem) and named once on screen with that emblem; slow rise, halo bloom (Indian, Jain and Buddhist figures; none for Greek, Roman or Norse gods), gold glint. High in the frame, never at foot level.
What is wanted, vowed or tested, made visible as objects (the bow, the churning rope, the golden apple); puppets act it in profile.
The threat or the cost: palette swap to vermilion and ink, embers, closer camera; violence implied by silhouette and cut, never gore.
Divine intervention, boon, curse or realisation, told with a reveal device: kaavad doors open, a scroll unrolls, the lamp is carried to the next scene.
The world changed: the opening composition returns altered (new light, blossoms falling, a figure missing).
What the tradition draws from the story, attributed ('the tradition reads this as ...'): one line, one image, a breath of stillness with the halo turning.
The lamp dims on the opening image; the source text and the image credits are on screen.

motion.signature: Paper placed by hand under a breathing lamp; the sacred figure rises slowly into its halo and is held, never bounced.
motion.continuous_layer: Lamp flicker on every scene, plus breathing and a turning halo on held sacred images and parallax drift between paper planes.
avoid: Bounce, squash or overshoot on a god, hero or sage.
Shattering, exploding, wiping or scattering a deity image.
Generic fantasy lighting (lens flares, neon) instead of lamp and gold.

rules.ending: Return to the opening lamp and composition, altered by the story; hold one image with breathing and flicker under a low drone; the source text and image credits are on screen.

short_form.closing: The return to the opening lamp doubles as the loop; the last line echoes the figure or object named in the hook.

anti_patterns.pattern: A deity image placed at foot level, on the ground plane, stepped over, dropped, shattered, glitched or wiped away.
anti_patterns.why: The Hindu American Foundation lists anything 'intended to be stepped upon' or 'likely to be destroyed' as offensive; the same holds for Buddha images in Buddhist practice. Keep sacred images high in the frame and remove them by dissolve or by lifting the paper away.
anti_patterns.source: research 2026-11-23: hinduamerican.org commercial-use guidelines; Buddha image etiquette (Tier 2, lankalens.com). .claude/skills/mythic-tales/references/traditions/

anti_patterns.pattern: An episode told without naming which telling it follows, or details mixed from two tellings.
anti_patterns.why: Valmiki, Kamban, Tulsidas and the Jain Ramayana differ in what Rama is and who kills Ravana (Ramanujan, 'Three Hundred Ramayanas'). The cartouche names the text and version; the research dossier holds the variants.
anti_patterns.source: research 2026-11-23: ruralindiaonline.org summary of A. K. Ramanujan

anti_patterns.pattern: Greek and Roman names mixed in one film, or a modern film or game portrayal used as the source (Marvel's Thor and Loki, winged Viking helmets, Disney's Hercules).
anti_patterns.why: Pick one naming tradition per film to match the source (Homer and Hesiod Greek, Ovid Roman). Loki is not Thor's brother in the Eddas; the winged helmet is an 1876 Wagner costume.
anti_patterns.source: research 2026-11-23: Prose Edda, Doepler costumes, Greek-Roman name charts

anti_patterns.pattern: Valknut, the Othala rune or the sonnenrad ('black sun') used as decoration or generic 'Norse' texture.
anti_patterns.why: All three are catalogued as appropriated hate symbols (ADL; The Conversation on the sonnenrad). Show them only when a historical artefact requires it, and say what it is.
anti_patterns.source: research 2026-11-23: ADL hate symbol database (valknot, othala-rune)

anti_patterns.pattern: A Tirthankara fighting, granting boons or protecting someone; a human Buddha in a scene set in the aniconic period; a Jataka told as the historical Buddha's biography.
anti_patterns.why: Jain tradition holds a Tirthankara is free of attachment and aversion; early Buddhist art shows the Buddha by throne, tree, wheel or footprints; Jatakas are previous-life teaching stories.
anti_patterns.source: research 2026-11-23: Smarthistory on mudras; aniconism in Buddhism; Jain lanchhana sources (Tier 2)

anti_patterns.pattern: 'Myth' used to mean 'false', a debunking aside, or a sermon telling the viewer what to believe.
anti_patterns.why: The stance is storyteller. Attribute belief and meaning ('Hindus regard Krishna as an avatar of Vishnu', 'the tradition reads this as ...'); never assert or deny it.

anti_patterns.pattern: A generated still of a god with the wrong attributes (number of arms, weapon, mount, emblem, skin colour) or a Tirthankara without the right lanchhana.
anti_patterns.why: Image models hallucinate iconography. Every generated figure passes the tradition pack's checklist and is logged as generated in the asset record; prefer a public-domain museum image.
anti_patterns.source: design profile mythic-storyteller weaknesses; owner brief 2026-11-23 (AI stills allowed, flagged)

anti_patterns.pattern: Raw stock photographs, or plates from different museums left in their own colours.
anti_patterns.why: Mixed photographs read as a slideshow. Duotone every plate to ink and paper, mount it with a margin or cut it out, and credit it.
anti_patterns.source: Authored from the design profile; not yet render-tested.

anti_patterns.pattern: Narration over a frame that does not change for more than max_beat_gap_sec, including on the sacred hold.
anti_patterns.why: Anti-laziness rule. A held deity keeps breathing, the halo turning and the lamp flickering, and a new detail (emblem label, glint, petal) lands every 2-3 s.
anti_patterns.source: CLAUDE.md anti-laziness rule; storybook anti-pattern evidence (review-top3-films-2026-11-03)

anti_patterns.pattern: Named or shown figures the viewer cannot identify (a god with no label, an emblem never explained).
anti_patterns.why: The viewer leaves able to recognise the figure by its emblems, so the first appearance names the figure and points at one emblem (Shiva's trident, the Mahavira lion, Odin's ravens).
anti_patterns.source: owner review of game-theory-trust 2026-11-07 (storybook anti-pattern), applied to iconography

reference_projects.note: 22 s silent portrait sample, Hanuman's leap, mythic-paper (local, projects/ is untracked).
Same storyboard, shadow-lantern: leather puppet on twos, lamp follows the leap.
Same storyboard, painted-folio: Pattachitra border, three registers read top-down.
Same storyboard, carved-relief: two CC0 Cleveland Museum of Art bronzes as plates, credited on screen.

open_questions: No film has been made to this template; every rule value is a first guess.
Palettes are estimated from pigment names, several from blog sources; measure against museum photographs when a film is made.
Who signs off iconography and telling for Jain and Buddhist films (JAINA, a scholar, a practitioner) is not decided.
Devanagari, Greek and runic display text need an @font-face project font; none is bundled with HyperFrames.

The figure library (kits/mythic/figures.js) holds eight stylised figures drawn from the tradition packs; none has had a tradition reviewer's sign-off yet (quality-rubric.md gate 2), and Devi, Durga, Krishna, Thor and Loki are not drawn yet.
